When you call set_content with a str that has non-ASCII text, the charset is always UTF-8 unless you
pass another one. The transfer encoding is picked by a heuristic in _encode_text. I read the code   
but didn't run it. The line numbers below come from the files in email/.                            

1. Dispatch                                                                                         

 • email/message.py:1214: EmailMessage.set_content calls super().set_content(...). Afterwards it    
   adds MIME-Version: 1.0 if it's missing (lines 1216–1217).                                        
 • email/message.py:1142-1145: MIMEPart.set_content uses self.policy.content_manager when you don't 
   pass one.                                                                                        
    • MIMEPart.__init__ (lines 991-995) defaults the policy to email.policy.default.                
    • That policy sets content_manager = raw_data_manager (email/policy.py:97).                     
 • email/contentmanager.py:31-38: ContentManager.set_content does three things.                     
    • It rejects multipart messages.                                                                
    • It finds a handler by walking the MRO of type(obj) (_find_set_handler, lines 40-59).          
    • It calls msg.clear_content() and then the handler.                                            
 • email/contentmanager.py:196: str is registered to set_text_content.                              

2. Charset                                                                                          

set_text_content is at email/contentmanager.py:185-195.                                             

 • The signature has charset='utf-8' and cte=None (line 185). So the charset is not detected from   
   the text. It is UTF-8 unless the caller says otherwise.                                          
 • Line 189 calls _encode_text(string, charset, cte, msg.policy).                                   
 • Lines 191-193 write the charset parameter, mapping it through email.charset.ALIASES.             
 • Line 194 sets Content-Transfer-Encoding to the cte that _encode_text returned.                   
 • Line 99 (_prepare_set) sets Content-Type: text/<subtype>.                                        

3. Transfer encoding: _encode_text (email/contentmanager.py:145-182)                                

The inputs are maxlen = policy.max_line_length or sys.maxsize (line 147). The default policy has    
max_line_length = 78 (_policybase.py:181) and cte_type = '8bit' (_policybase.py:180). lines =       
string.encode(charset).splitlines() (line 148) encodes the text to bytes first.                     

If cte is None, which is the default (line 152), the choice goes in this order:                     

 1 7bit (lines 154-158). If the longest line is within maxlen and the body decodes as ASCII, it     
   returns '7bit'. Non-ASCII text fails this check.                                                 
 2 8bit (lines 159-160). If all lines fit within maxlen and policy.cte_type == '8bit', it returns   
   '8bit'. The bytes are decoded with surrogateescape so the raw bytes stay in the str payload. This
   is the default policy, so short-line UTF-8 text normally ends up as 8bit.                        
 3 Quoted-printable or base64 (lines 161-170). This is reached if a line is too long, or if the     
   policy's cte_type is '7bit', as in a custom 7bit policy.                                         
    • It takes the first 10 lines as a sample (sniff, line 161).                                    
    • It encodes the sample both ways: sniff_qp with quoprimime.body_encode (line 162) and          
      sniff_base64 with binascii.b2a_base64 (line 163).                                             
    • If QP is longer than base64, it picks base64 (lines 165-166). Otherwise it picks              
      quoted-printable (line 168), and if there are 10 lines or fewer it returns the sample's QP    
      form directly (lines 169-170).                                                                

The actual encoding happens at lines 171-181:                                                       

 • 7bit or 8bit: the lines are joined with \n.                                                      
 • quoted-printable: quoprimime.body_encode(..., maxlen) runs on the latin-1 view of the bytes (line
   176). body_encode is at quoprimime.py:153. It escapes special characters and soft-wraps lines    
   with =.                                                                                          
 • base64: the code calls _encode_base64 (lines 136-142). It splits the data into chunks of         
   maxlen//4*3 bytes and encodes each chunk. The joined lines use the policy's linesep              
   (embedded_body, line 150).                                                                       
 • Explicit cte: if you pass cte= yourself, the heuristic is skipped. A cte of '7bit' with non-ASCII
   text raises, because the ASCII decode at line 172 fails. A cte that isn't one of the four known  
   values raises ValueError (line 181).                                                             

The payload is then stored with msg.set_payload(payload) (line 190).                                

4. Final bytes: the generator                                                                       

as_bytes (message.py:202-213) uses BytesGenerator, which goes through Generator._write              
(generator.py:~170-204).                                                                            

 1 Body first. The body is written into a buffer by _dispatch (lines 182-183, 206-220). For text/*  
   it calls _handle_text.                                                                           
 2 Surrogate check. BytesGenerator._handle_text (generator.py:446-456) checks the payload for       
   surrogates.                                                                                      
    • This applies to the 8bit case, where the payload holds surrogate-escaped bytes.               
    • If the policy isn't 7bit, it writes the payload straight out (lines 451-454).                 
      BytesGenerator.write (line 421) does s.encode('ascii', 'surrogateescape'), which turns the    
      surrogates back into the original UTF-8 bytes.                                                
    • Otherwise it falls to Generator._handle_text (lines 245-264).

   known, the message is deep-copied and re-encoded with set_payload(..., charset) (lines 251-259). 
   It records _munge_cte (lines 260-261), and lines 189-196 then rewrite the headers to match.      
 4 Line endings. _write_lines (generator.py:151-160) converts line endings to the policy's linesep. 
 5 Headers. After the body, _write_headers (lines 429-444) writes the headers via                   
   policy.fold_binary. Content-Type: text/plain; charset="utf-8" and Content-Transfer-Encoding: ... 
   come out as ASCII. The code writes a blank line, then the buffered body (generator.py:204).

 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 
 Default policy, all lines ≤ 78 bytes          8bit, raw UTF-8 bytes

Short answer: set_content never detects a charset. It uses utf-8 unless you pass charset=. The CTE  
comes from a size and ASCII heuristic in _encode_text. The generator changes it later only if the   
policy requires 7bit.                                                                               

All paths are relative to /private/tmp/mail.                                                        

1. Entry point                                                                                      

 • email/message.py:1214-1217: EmailMessage.set_content calls super().set_content(...). It then adds
   MIME-Version: 1.0 if that header is missing.                                                     
 • email/message.py:1142-1145: MIMEPart.set_content takes the content_manager argument or falls back
   to self.policy.content_manager. It then calls content_manager.set_content(self, *args, **kw).    
 • email/policy.py:97: the default EmailPolicy.content_manager is raw_data_manager.                 

2. Handler dispatch                                                                                 

 • email/contentmanager.py:31-38: ContentManager.set_content does four things:                      
    • It rejects multipart messages.                                                                
    • It looks up a handler with _find_set_handler (lines 40-59), which walks type(obj).__mro__.    
    • It calls msg.clear_content().                                                                 
    • It calls the handler.                                                                         
 • A str resolves to set_text_content, registered at line 196.                                      

3. Charset choice                                                                                   

email/contentmanager.py:185-195: set_text_content(msg, string, subtype="plain", charset='utf-8',    
cte=None, …).                                                                                       

 • The charset is just the charset='utf-8' default in the signature, or whatever the caller passes. 
 • Line 191-193 writes it to the charset parameter of Content-Type. The name is normalized through  
   email.charset.ALIASES.                                                                           
 • _prepare_set (lines 98-112) sets Content-Type: text/<subtype> first.                             

4. CTE choice                                                                                       

Line 189 calls _encode_text(string, charset, cte, msg.policy) (lines 145-182). It first encodes the 
string with the charset and splits it into lines. The limit is maxlen = policy.max_line_length or   
sys.maxsize, which is 78 by default (email/_policybase.py:181).                                     

With cte=None, it tries these in order:                                                             

 1 7bit (lines 154-158). It applies when every line is ≤ maxlen and the bytes decode as ASCII.      
 2 8bit (lines 159-160). It applies when the lines fit, the text is non-ASCII, and policy.cte_type  
   == '8bit'. That is the default (_policybase.py:180). The payload is stored as a                  
   surrogateescape-decoded str.                                                                     
 3 Otherwise, meaning a line is too long or cte_type == '7bit' (lines 161-170):                     
    • It takes the first 10 lines and builds both a quoted-printable version                        
      (quoprimime.body_encode) and a base64 version (b2a_base64).                                   
    • If QP is longer than base64, it picks base64.                                                 
    • Otherwise it picks quoted-printable. If the text has ≤10 lines, it returns the sniffed QP text
      directly.                                                                                     

With an explicit cte (lines 171-182):                                                               

 • 7bit and 8bit are encoded as above.                                                              
 • quoted-printable uses quoprimime.body_encode(..., maxlen).                                       
 • base64 uses _encode_base64 (lines 136-142), which takes max_line_length // 4 * 3 input bytes per 
   line.                                                                                            
 • Any other value raises ValueError.                                                               

Back in set_text_content, line 190 stores the payload with msg.set_payload(payload). Line 194 sets  
Content-Transfer-Encoding. _finalize_set (lines 115-129) handles disposition, filename, cid and     
params.                                                                                             

5. Serialization to bytes (email/generator.py)                                                      

 • Generator.flatten calls _write(msg) at line 118.                                                 
 • _write (lines 167-204) renders the body into a buffer first, via _dispatch at line 183. It then  
   writes the headers (lines 199-203) and the buffer (line 204).                                    
 • _dispatch (lines 206-220) sends text/plain to _handle_text (lines 245-264).                      
 • Str Generator, _handle_text, line 251: if the payload has surrogates (the 8bit case) and a       
   charset is set, it does the following:                                                           
    • It deep-copies the message and deletes the CTE header.                                        
    • It calls set_payload(payload, charset), which lets email.charset re-encode the text, usually  
      to base64 or QP.                                                                              
    • It records _munge_cte (lines 260-261). _write applies it at lines 186-196 to replace the CTE  
      and Content-Type headers.                                                                     
 • BytesGenerator (line 407 onward):                                                                
    • write (line 421) does s.encode('ascii', 'surrogateescape'), which turns the surrogates back   
      into raw 8-bit bytes.                                                                         
    • _handle_text (lines 446-456) writes surrogate payloads unchanged when policy.cte_type !=      
      '7bit'. So with default settings an 8bit body goes out as raw UTF-8 bytes with                
      Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit.                                                              
    • With cte_type == '7bit', it falls back to the str _handle_text path above, so the body is     
      re-encoded to QP or base64.

When you call `set_content` with a `str` that has non-ASCII text, the charset is always UTF-8 unless you pass another one. The transfer encoding is picked by a heuristic in `_encode_text`. I read the code but didn't run it. The line numbers below come from the files in `email/`.

## 1. Dispatch

- **`email/message.py:1214`**: `EmailMessage.set_content` calls `super().set_content(...)`. Afterwards it adds `MIME-Version: 1.0` if it's missing (lines 1216–1217).
- **`email/message.py:1142-1145`**: `MIMEPart.set_content` uses `self.policy.content_manager` when you don't pass one.
  - `MIMEPart.__init__` (lines 991-995) defaults the policy to `email.policy.default`.
  - That policy sets `content_manager = raw_data_manager` (`email/policy.py:97`).
- **`email/contentmanager.py:31-38`**: `ContentManager.set_content` does three things.
  - It rejects multipart messages.
  - It finds a handler by walking the MRO of `type(obj)` (`_find_set_handler`, lines 40-59).
  - It calls `msg.clear_content()` and then the handler.
- **`email/contentmanager.py:196`**: `str` is registered to `set_text_content`.

## 2. Charset

`set_text_content` is at `email/contentmanager.py:185-195`.

- The signature has `charset='utf-8'` and `cte=None` (line 185). So the charset is not detected from the text. It is UTF-8 unless the caller says otherwise.
- Line 189 calls `_encode_text(string, charset, cte, msg.policy)`.
- Lines 191-193 write the charset parameter, mapping it through `email.charset.ALIASES`.
- Line 194 sets `Content-Transfer-Encoding` to the `cte` that `_encode_text` returned.
- Line 99 (`_prepare_set`) sets `Content-Type: text/<subtype>`.

## 3. Transfer encoding: `_encode_text` (`email/contentmanager.py:145-182`)

The inputs are `maxlen = policy.max_line_length or sys.maxsize` (line 147). The default policy has `max_line_length = 78` (`_policybase.py:181`) and `cte_type = '8bit'` (`_policybase.py:180`). `lines = string.encode(charset).splitlines()` (line 148) encodes the text to bytes first.

If `cte is None`, which is the default (line 152), the choice goes in this order:

1. **7bit** (lines 154-158). If the longest line is within `maxlen` and the body decodes as ASCII, it returns `'7bit'`. Non-ASCII text fails this check.
2. **8bit** (lines 159-160). If all lines fit within `maxlen` and `policy.cte_type == '8bit'`, it returns `'8bit'`. The bytes are decoded with `surrogateescape` so the raw bytes stay in the str payload. This is the default policy, so **short-line UTF-8 text normally ends up as 8bit**.
3. **Quoted-printable or base64** (lines 161-170). This is reached if a line is too long, or if the policy's `cte_type` is `'7bit'`, as in a custom 7bit policy.
   - It takes the first 10 lines as a sample (`sniff`, line 161).
   - It encodes the sample both ways: `sniff_qp` with `quoprimime.body_encode` (line 162) and `sniff_base64` with `binascii.b2a_base64` (line 163).
   - If QP is longer than base64, it picks `base64` (lines 165-166). Otherwise it picks `quoted-printable` (line 168), and if there are 10 lines or fewer it returns the sample's QP form directly (lines 169-170).

The actual encoding happens at lines 171-181:
- **`7bit` or `8bit`:** the lines are joined with `\n`.

**Short answer:** `set_content` never detects a charset. It uses `utf-8` unless you pass `charset=`. The CTE comes from a size and ASCII heuristic in `_encode_text`. The generator changes it later only if the policy requires 7bit.

All paths are relative to `/private/tmp/mail`.

## 1. Entry point
- `email/message.py:1214-1217`: `EmailMessage.set_content` calls `super().set_content(...)`. It then adds `MIME-Version: 1.0` if that header is missing.
- `email/message.py:1142-1145`: `MIMEPart.set_content` takes the `content_manager` argument or falls back to `self.policy.content_manager`. It then calls `content_manager.set_content(self, *args, **kw)`.
- `email/policy.py:97`: the default `EmailPolicy.content_manager` is `raw_data_manager`.

## 2. Handler dispatch
- `email/contentmanager.py:31-38`: `ContentManager.set_content` does four things:
  - It rejects multipart messages.
  - It looks up a handler with `_find_set_handler` (lines 40-59), which walks `type(obj).__mro__`.
  - It calls `msg.clear_content()`.
  - It calls the handler.
- A `str` resolves to `set_text_content`, registered at line 196.

## 3. Charset choice
`email/contentmanager.py:185-195`: `set_text_content(msg, string, subtype="plain", charset='utf-8', cte=None, …)`.
- The charset is just the `charset='utf-8'` default in the signature, or whatever the caller passes.
- Line 191-193 writes it to the `charset` parameter of Content-Type. The name is normalized through `email.charset.ALIASES`.
- `_prepare_set` (lines 98-112) sets `Content-Type: text/<subtype>` first.

## 4. CTE choice
Line 189 calls `_encode_text(string, charset, cte, msg.policy)` (lines 145-182). It first encodes the string with the charset and splits it into lines. The limit is `maxlen = policy.max_line_length or sys.maxsize`, which is 78 by default (`email/_policybase.py:181`).

With `cte=None`, it tries these in order:
1. **`7bit`** (lines 154-158). It applies when every line is ≤ `maxlen` and the bytes decode as ASCII.
2. **`8bit`** (lines 159-160). It applies when the lines fit, the text is non-ASCII, and `policy.cte_type == '8bit'`. That is the default (`_policybase.py:180`). The payload is stored as a `surrogateescape`-decoded str.
3. **Otherwise**, meaning a line is too long or `cte_type == '7bit'` (lines 161-170):
   - It takes the first 10 lines and builds both a quoted-printable version (`quoprimime.body_encode`) and a base64 version (`b2a_base64`).
   - If QP is longer than base64, it picks `base64`.
   - Otherwise it picks `quoted-printable`. If the text has ≤10 lines, it returns the sniffed QP text directly.

With an explicit `cte` (lines 171-182):
- `7bit` and `8bit` are encoded as above.
- `quoted-printable` uses `quoprimime.body_encode(..., maxlen)`.
- `base64` uses `_encode_base64` (lines 136-142), which takes `max_line_length // 4 * 3` input bytes per line.
- Any other value raises `ValueError`.

Back in `set_text_content`, line 190 stores the payload with `msg.set_payload(payload)`. Line 194 sets `Content-Transfer-Encoding`. `_finalize_set` (lines 115-129) handles disposition, filename, cid and params.

## 5. Serialization to bytes (`email/generator.py`)
- `Generator.flatten` calls `_write(msg)` at line 118.
- `_write` (lines 167-204) renders the body into a buffer first, via `_dispatch` at line 183. It then writes the headers (lines 199-203) and the buffer (line 204).
- `_dispatch` (lines 206-220) sends `text/plain` to `_handle_text` (lines 245-264).
- **Str `Generator`, `_handle_text`, line 251:** if the payload has surrogates (the 8bit case) and a charset is set, it does the following:
  - It deep-copies the message and deletes the CTE header.
  - It calls `set_payload(payload, charset)`, which lets `email.charset` re-encode the text, usually to base64 or QP.
  - It records `_munge_cte` (lines 260-261). `_write` applies it at lines 186-196 to replace the CTE and Content-Type headers.
- **`BytesGenerator`** (line 407 onward):
  - `write` (line 421) does `s.encode('ascii', 'surrogateescape')`, which turns the surrogates back into raw 8-bit bytes.
  - `_handle_text` (lines 446-456) writes surrogate payloads unchanged when `policy.cte_type != '7bit'`. So with default settings an 8bit body goes out as raw UTF-8 bytes with `Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit`.
  - With `cte_type == '7bit'`, it falls back to the str `_handle_text` path above, so the body is re-encoded to QP or base64.

| Situation | Charset | CTE on the wire |
|---|---|---|
| ASCII, short lines | `utf-8` (default) | `7bit` |

| Non-ASCII, `cte_type='7bit'` policy, or a line over 78 characters | `utf-8` | `base64` or `quoted-printable`, whichever the size comparison favors |

`set_content` doesn't choose the charset. It defaults to `utf-8`, and the caller can override it with `charset=`. The transfer encoding is chosen by a heuristic in `_encode_text`. I read the code but didn't run it.

## Call path

1. **`email/message.py:1214`**: `EmailMessage.set_content` calls `super().set_content(...)`. After that it adds `MIME-Version: 1.0` if it's missing (lines 1216-1217).
2. **`email/message.py:1142-1145`**: `MIMEPart.set_content` takes `self.policy.content_manager` when none is passed. For the default policy that is `raw_data_manager` (`email/policy.py:97`). It then calls `content_manager.set_content(self, ...)`.
3. **`email/contentmanager.py:31-38`**: `ContentManager.set_content` rejects multipart messages. It looks up a handler by the type of `obj` (`_find_set_handler`, line 40), calls `msg.clear_content()` and then calls the handler. For a `str`, the handler is `set_text_content`, registered at line 196.
4. **`email/contentmanager.py:185-195`**: `set_text_content` does the following:
   - The signature at line 185 is where the charset default comes from: `charset='utf-8'` and `cte=None`.
   - `_prepare_set` (line 188) sets `Content-Type: text/plain`.
   - Line 189 calls `_encode_text(string, charset, cte, msg.policy)`. That returns the chosen `(cte, payload)`.
   - Line 190 calls `msg.set_payload(payload)`. No charset is passed, so `message.py:349-352` stores the string as is.
   - Lines 191-193 write `charset=utf-8` into the Content-Type header. `email.charset.ALIASES` normalizes the name.
   - Line 194 sets `Content-Transfer-Encoding` to the chosen value.

## The transfer-encoding decision: `_encode_text`, `contentmanager.py:145-182`

- **Line 147:** `maxlen = policy.max_line_length or sys.maxsize`. The default max line length is 78 (`_policybase.py:181`).
- **Line 148:** `lines = string.encode(charset).splitlines()`. The text becomes bytes in the chosen charset, and the encoding decision is made on those bytes.
- **Lines 152-160, with `cte=None`:** if every line is at most `maxlen`:
  - It tries 7bit by decoding the body as ASCII (lines 156-158). That fails for non-ASCII text.
  - If `policy.cte_type == '8bit'`, it returns `'8bit'` (lines 159-160). The body is decoded with `surrogateescape`, so the raw bytes ride inside a `str`. The default policy has `cte_type = '8bit'` (`_policybase.py:180`), so short non-ASCII text usually ends up as 8bit.
- **Lines 161-168, otherwise (a line is too long, or the policy is 7bit):**
  - It takes the first 10 lines as a sample.
  - It encodes the sample both ways, as quoted-printable (`quoprimime.body_encode`, line 162) and as base64 (line 163).
  - If QP is longer than base64, it picks `base64` (line 166). Otherwise it picks `quoted-printable`.
  - If the QP choice has 10 lines or fewer, it returns the sample's QP output directly (lines 169-170).
- **Lines 171-181:** this does the actual encoding for the cases not already returned:
  - 7bit and 8bit use `normal_body`.
  - `quoted-printable` uses `quoprimime.body_encode` (line 176).
  - `base64` uses `_encode_base64` (lines 136-142, line 179), which calls `binascii.b2a_base64` on chunks.
  - An unknown value raises `ValueError`.
- **Explicit `cte=`:** passing `cte='base64'` (or another value) skips the heuristic block and goes straight to the branches at lines 171-181.

## Final bytes: `msg.as_bytes()` or `bytes(msg)`

1. **`message.py:197-215`**: `as_bytes` creates a `BytesGenerator` and calls `flatten`. `_write` (`generator.py:167+`) renders the body first (line 183, `_dispatch`) and the headers after it (lines 199-204).
2. **`generator.py:206-220`**: `_dispatch` picks `_handle_text` for `text/plain`.
3. **`generator.py:446-456`**: `BytesGenerator._handle_text` checks the payload.
   - **8bit case:** the payload contains surrogates and the policy isn't 7bit (line 451). It calls `_write_lines` (line 454), and `write` (line 421) turns the surrogates back into the original raw bytes with `s.encode('ascii','surrogateescape')`.
   - **7bit, QP or base64 case:** the payload is plain ASCII. It goes through `Generator._handle_text` (line 456, which runs `generator.py:245-264`) and is written unchanged.
4. **`generator.py:429-444`**: `_write_headers` folds each header with `policy.fold_binary` (`policy.py:193-209`) and writes it to the stream. This is where `Content-Type: text/plain; charset="utf-8"` and `Content-Transfer-Encoding: ...` come out.

## Caveats

- **`str` output (`as_string()` / `Generator`):** `Generator._handle_text` (`generator.py:251-261`) sees the surrogates from the 8bit case. It re-runs `set_payload(payload, charset)` with a `Charset` object, which re-encodes the body using the charset's own body-encoding rule. I didn't read `charset.py`, so I haven't confirmed which encoding that picks. The result can differ from what `_encode_text` chose, and `_munge_cte` records the change.
- **Mixed line endings:** the QP shortcut at line 170 uses `embedded_body`, which joins lines with `policy.linesep`. The other paths use `\n` and leave the conversion to the generator.
